summary: Return the k elements of a sorted array closest to x (ties prefer the smaller value), in ascending order.
mainInsight: The k closest elements of a sorted array form a contiguous window. Binary search its start by comparing the element about to leave on the left with the element about to enter on the right.
invariant: The best window start lies in [lo, hi] at the start of every iteration.
canonicalApproach: Binary search on the window start

approaches.name: Sort by distance
approaches.summary: Sort by (distance, value), take k, sort the result.

approaches.name: Two pointers shrinking
approaches.summary: Drop whichever end of the array is farther from x until k remain.

approaches.name: Binary search on the window start
approaches.summary: Search i in [0, n - k] using x - arr[i] versus arr[i + k] - x.

approaches.name: Insertion point then expand
approaches.summary: Binary search for x, expand two pointers outward k times.

personalSolution.approach: Binary search for x's insertion point, then expand two pointers k times
personalSolution.notes: Optimal complexity. Searching the window start directly (canonical) avoids the three-way branching at the array boundaries.

commonMistakes: Using >= in the comparison, which breaks the tie rule.
Searching up to n - 1 so arr[mid + k] goes out of range.
Forgetting that the output must be sorted (the slice already is).

promptVariants: Why is the answer always a contiguous block of the array?
What does a comparison at the window boundary tell you?
cards.answer: In a sorted array, distance to x decreases then increases, so if a value is among the k closest then every value between it and x is also at least as close. Hence the k closest form a block arr[i : i + k]. For a candidate start mid, compare the first element of the window with the first element after it: if arr[mid + k] is closer to x, the window must slide right; otherwise it can stay or move left.
keyPoints: Distance is unimodal in a sorted array
Answer is a window of length k
cards.explanation: Searching the window start turns the problem into a one-dimensional binary search.

promptVariants: Why does the search run over [0, len(arr) - k] rather than [0, len(arr) - 1]?
What is the largest valid start of the window and why?
options: A window starting after n - k would run past the end of the array
A window starting after n - k would contain elements farther than x
The last k elements are always the closest ones to x in the array
The upper bound keeps mid + k from equalling the array length by chance
cards.answer: A window starting after n - k would run past the end of the array
cards.explanation: The window [i, i + k) needs i + k <= n, so i <= n - k. It also keeps arr[mid + k] a valid index since mid < hi <= n - k.

incorrectOptionExplanations.A window starting after n - k would cont: Distance has nothing to do with the bound; it is an array length limit.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The last k elements are always the close: They are only the closest if x is larger than every element.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The upper bound keeps mid + k from equal: mid < hi <= n - k guarantees mid + k <= n - 1, which is a structural fact.

promptVariants: Which test moves the window right at mid in the canonical code?
What comparison decides between window [mid, mid + k) and [mid + 1, mid + k + 1)?
cards.explanation: The windows differ by dropping arr[mid] and adding arr[mid + k]; the right-shifted window is better exactly when the added element is strictly closer to x.

incorrectOptionExplanations.arr[mid] < x: Only says arr[mid] is left of x, not that the next window is better.
incorrectOptionExplanations.arr[mid + k] > x: Says the new element is right of x, but not that it is closer than arr[mid].
incorrectOptionExplanations.abs(arr[mid] - x) < abs(arr[mid + k - 1]: That compares with an element that stays in both windows.

promptVariants: For arr = [1, 3], k = 1, x = 2, what happens if the comparison uses >= instead of >?
How does changing the strict > to >= affect ties?
options: It returns [3] and violates the tie rule, which prefers the smaller value
It returns [1] and violates the tie rule, which prefers the larger value
It returns [1, 3] because both are equally close to the target
It loops forever because lo never reaches hi on a tie
cards.answer: It returns [3] and violates the tie rule, which prefers the smaller value
cards.explanation: 1 and 3 are both at distance 1 from 2. The statement says the smaller value wins ties, so we must not slide right on equality; with >= the window slides to [3].

incorrectOptionExplanations.It returns [1] and violates the tie rule: The tie rule prefers the smaller value, and [1] is what the correct code returns.
incorrectOptionExplanations.It returns [1, 3] because both are equal: The answer always has exactly k = 1 elements.
incorrectOptionExplanations.It loops forever because lo never reache: lo or hi moves on every iteration, so it terminates.

promptVariants: In your expansion loop, why is the comparison `x - arr[left] <= arr[right] - x` and not `<`?
What does the tie case of your expansion step decide?
cards.answer: On a tie both elements are equally close, and the statement prefers the smaller value, which is arr[left]. Taking left when the distances are equal implements that rule; with strict < a tie would take arr[right] and return larger values.
keyPoints: <= takes the left element on ties
cards.explanation: Tie-breaking rules are common sources of off-by-one-style bugs.

promptVariants: What is the time complexity of the canonical code?
Derive the running time from the loop and the slice.
cards.explanation: The binary search halves a range of size n - k + 1, and the final slice copies k elements.

incorrectOptionExplanations.O(n log n): That is the cost of sorting by distance.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(n): The search is logarithmic and only the output is linear in k.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(k log n): A single binary search is performed, not one per output element.
